analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health program covering every American with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The single-payer health bill was introduced by Senator Paul Wellstone and three Senate colleagues on March 3, 1993, sent to the Finance Committee, and never received a vote or a committee markup before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, and private health insurance with a single government-run program administered by the states, covering every U.S. resident for hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, mental health, substance abuse treatment, dental, vision, and long-term care — with no deductibles, copays, or balance billing. Hospitals would be paid through fixed annual budgets, drug prices would be negotiated by a federal board, and private insurers would be barred from selling duplicate coverage. The program would be financed by higher individual and corporate income taxes, a surtax on incomes over $1 million, and higher payroll taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident: the roughly 38 million then-uninsured, plus insured people who would stop paying premiums, deductibles, and copays. Rural and underserved communities would gain expanded primary care funding, and the elderly would gain coverage for prescription drugs and home-based long-term care that Medicare largely did not cover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured Americans; people paying premiums

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a universal entitlement: every citizen, national, and lawful resident alien is entitled to comprehensive health benefits under a state-administered American Health Security Program [S2][S3].

Bans all deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments, prohibits providers from billing patients beyond the program's payment, and bars the sale of private insurance that duplicates program benefits [S2][S3].

Covers services private plans often excluded or capped, including prescription drugs, mental health, substance abuse treatment, dental and vision care, and home and community-based long-term care capped at 65% of nursing-home cost [S2][S3].

Supersedes and folds in Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS as of January 1, 1995, while leaving veterans' VA care and Indian Health Service benefits untouched [S2][S3].

Finances the program through an American Health Security Trust Fund fed by higher individual and corporate income taxes, a surtax on incomes over $1 million, and increased hospital-insurance (Medicare payroll) taxes [S2][S3].
Directs funding to medically underserved areas through community health center grants, primary care training goals, and payment incentives for practitioners in shortage areas [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally through higher income, corporate, and payroll taxes; individuals earning over $1 million through a new surtax; high-income households through permanent limits on itemized deductions and personal exemptions; businesses through higher hospital-insurance taxes and loss of drug and oil-and-gas tax breaks; and health insurers and drug manufacturers through loss of revenue and government-negotiated prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, high earners, insurers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The financing falls on broad tax bases: higher individual and corporate income tax rates, a health security premium, increased employer hospital-insurance taxes (newly covering state and local employees), and higher estimated tax payments — a substantial and permanent tax increase [S2][S3].

Hospitals and nursing facilities would be paid under fixed annual global budgets, and new building or equipment purchases would require prior government approval, with services tied to unapproved capital spending not covered at all — a constraint hospitals argued could delay new technology [S2].

A federal board would classify prescription drugs and negotiate maximum prices with manufacturers, and set coverage limits on eyeglasses, hearing aids, and equipment — giving a national board sweeping power over what care is covered and at what price [S2].

Mental health and substance abuse treatment beyond 20 outpatient visits or 15 inpatient days per year would be subject to utilization review, and the bill's national health budget could not grow faster than the economy, so benefits would depend on tight annual cost controls [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the trade is large: paying taxes instead of premiums, deductibles, and copays, with no gaps in coverage — a deal most uninsured and underinsured families would gain from, since U.S. health spending per person already exceeded what other universal-coverage countries paid. The costs are real but concentrated: higher taxes on high earners and corporations, eliminated revenue for insurers, and government-set budgets and prices for hospitals and drug makers. The main design risk is the fixed national budget growing no faster than GDP, which would force hard choices about new technology and the pace of spending growth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 3, 1993, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up — no markup, no floor vote — so it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone of Minnesota introduced the bill on March 3, 1993, joined by Senators Metzenbaum, Simon, and Inouye [S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; the only subsequent action was the ordering of a star print (a corrected reprint) on March 9, 1993 [S5].
No committee markup, hearing-based consideration leading to a vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill received no further action before the 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

With only five sponsors, all Democrats, the bill sat in committee during the 1993–94 period when Congress debated the Clinton administration's health reform proposal and more moderate alternatives, none of which were a single government-run program.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and other health industries that would have lost revenue under a single government program were better off because the bill died; the employer-based insurance system continued unchanged, and tens of millions of uninsured and underinsured Americans remained outside guaranteed coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the employer-insurance status quo

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Health Security Act of 1993 and delivered introductory remarks on March 3, 1993

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 3, 1993 and never scheduled a markup or brought it to a vote; it died there when the Congress ended

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers whose duplicate-coverage business the bill would have abolished
against.what_they_did: Funded a large public campaign against government-run health care during the 1993–94 reform debate, including the well-known 'Harry and Louise' advertising campaign

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred so no party split is recorded; all five sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined.

industries.note: The bill prohibits selling any private insurance that duplicates program benefits and folds the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program into the public plan, effectively eliminating the core of the private health insurance industry. Insurers' revenue came from the premiums and cost-sharing the bill abolished, so their interest ran directly against guaranteed no-cost-sharing coverage for the public.

A federal board would classify drugs and negotiate maximum prices with manufacturers, replacing market pricing for a national customer base. Drug makers would gain universal coverage as a customer but lose pricing power, and their interest in high prices was directly against patients' cost.

Hospitals would be paid through fixed annual global budgets with government approval required for capital spending, ending cost-shifting to private insurers but also ending uncompensated care for the uninsured. Guaranteed payment for everyone they treated came at the cost of centrally set budgets.

Every independent practitioner would be entitled to a fee for each covered service with no uncompensated care, but fee schedules would be set through negotiation under a national relative value scale, and balance billing would be banned. Guaranteed payment replaced charging power.

A new surtax on incomes over $1 million, permanent limits on itemized deductions and personal exemptions for high earners, permanent top estate and gift tax rates, and taxation of more Social Security benefits would fall on high-income households. The revenue funds coverage for people of all incomes.
The bill repeals the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion for oil and gas wells, and like-kind exchange treatment for real property, raising industry taxes to fund the trust fund.

Employers would stop paying most private health premiums but face a higher hospital-insurance (payroll) tax and higher corporate income taxes; many employers paying premiums would come out ahead, while low-premium or uninsured-payroll employers would pay more.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net providers
industries.note: The bill directs trust-fund revenue to community and migrant health centers, public health block grants, and grants for primary care centers serving underserved urban and rural areas, and pays for care for every enrolled person instead of uncompensated care.
